doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

chapter: Race and the nature of jazz
title: Race, Lincoln Center, and jazz as a merging of cultures
summary: Racial harmony among players, a UCLA clinic question, and his view that jazz merged African-American, European and Creole music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there any kind of racial disharmony in the music these days that you’re aware of with the players? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

I think there is a little bit but I really haven’t experienced any of it, okay. I have seen situations where — well I don’t want to criticize anyone, but I mean a situation like the Lincoln Center Jazz Ensemble that Wynton Marsalis has, and they’re trying to do more traditional jazz, and many of the guys are not that familiar with the traditional styles of music but they are given the job because they are not white players, they are black players. I think that’s unfortunate. But in all the traveling that I do and all the guys that I’ve worked with over the years, black or white, everybody is always on everybody else’s side. I mean Wendell Brunious is here, Wendell is a wonderful player. I love working with Wendell, he plays great. I mean Ray Brown, a monster.
Yeah this festival seems to be —

I don’t really — and I’ve traveled with Milt Hinton extensively and Milt is the most wonderful guy in the world and always very supportive. On a one-to-one basis I have never experienced it I’m happy to say. And I hope that it would be less and less as time goes on. Because I have experienced — I was in a thing with doing a clinic a year or so ago at UCLA with Kenny Burrell and guys were asking us questions, and this one guy kept saying, “Since jazz is an African-American art form, I mean where do you get off playing this music” and this kind of thing. And I really had to say to the guy, you know, your history’s a little off. Because jazz is not an African-American art form. What it is that makes it uniquely American is it’s a merging of African-American music and European music, and that’s what made it more unique, plus Creole influences of New Orleans. And because it all happened in New Orleans and the merging of all these different styles of music, that’s what created it. That’s what made it uniquely American. I said it’s not just the music of one race. That’s what’s so great about it. It’s exactly the opposite of everything that was going on in the south at the time.
That’s a good point. And depending on what history writer you read, sometimes you’ll get that opinion and sometimes you won’t.
